{{Nihongo|'''Kashii-gū'''|香椎宮|}} is a [[Shinto]] {{ill|Shinto shrine|abstract|Q845945|ar|جينجا|arz|ضريح شنتو|bcl|Shinto shrine|ca|Jinja|cs|Šintoistická svatyně|da|Shinto-tempel|de|Shintō-Schrein|el|Σιντοϊστικό Ιερό|eo|Ŝintoa sanktejo|es|Jinja|eu|Jinja|fa|معبد شینتویی|fi|Šintolainen pyhäkkö|fr|Sanctuaire shinto|hi|शिंतो मंदिर|hr|Šintoistički hram|hu|Sintó szentély|id|Jinja|it|Jinja|ja|神社|ka|ძინძია|ko|신사 (신토)|lb|Shintō-Schräin|mr|शिंतो मंदिर|nl|Jinja (heiligdom)|no|Jinja|or|ଜିଞ୍ଜା|pl|Jinja|pt|Templo xintoísta|ru|Дзиндзя|sc|Jinja|simple|Shinto shrine|sl|Šintoistično svetišče|sr|Шинтоистички храм|sv|Jinja|th|ศาลเจ้าชินโต|tok|tomo sewi pi nasin sewi Sinto|tr|Şinto tapınağı|uk|Святилище (синто)|uz|Dzindzya|vi|Thần xã|wuu|神社|zh|神社|zh_yue|神社|qid=Q845945|lt=shrine}} in {{ill|Higashi-ku, Fukuoka|ceb|Higashi Ku (subdistrito sa Hapon, Fukuoka-ken)|cs|Higaši-ku (Fukuoka)|es|Higashi-ku (Fukuoka)|fa|هیگاشی-کو، فوکوئوکا|fi|Higashi-ku (Fukuoka)|fr|Higashi-ku (Fukuoka)|id|Higashi-ku, Fukuoka|it|Higashi-ku (Fukuoka)|ja|東区 (福岡市)|ko|히가시구 (후쿠오카시)|pl|Higashi (Fukuoka)|th|เขตฮิงาชิ (ฟูกูโอกะ)|tr|Higashi, Fukuoka|ur|ہیگاشی وارڈ، فوکوکا|vi|Higashi, Fukuoka|zh|東區 (福岡市)|zh_yue|東區 (福岡市)|qid=Q1206659}}, {{ill|Japan|en|Japan|qid=Q17|lt=Japan}}. It worships {{ill|Emperor Chūai|en|Emperor Chūai|qid=Q179971|lt=Emperor Chūai}} and {{ill|Empress Jingū|en|Empress Jingū|qid=Q232803|lt=Empress Jingū}}.<ref name="VISIT FUKUOKA -Fukuoka Prefecture Official Travel Guide">{{Cite web|title=Kashii-gu Shrine|url=https://www.crossroadfukuoka.jp/en/spot/12512|access-date=2024-03-28|website=VISIT FUKUOKA -Fukuoka Prefecture Official Travel Guide|language=en|qq=draft}}</ref>

It is one of the Three Great Shrines of Northern Kyushu, alongside [[Usa Jingū]], and {{ill|Sumiyoshi Shrine (Fukuoka)|abstract|Q29682|de|Sumiyoshi-Schrein (Fukuoka)|fr|Sumiyoshi-jinja (Fukuoka)|ja|住吉神社 (福岡市)|simple|Sumiyoshi Shrine (Fukuoka)|zh|住吉神社 (福岡市)|qid=Q29682|lt=Sumiyoshi Shrine}}.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://www.amazon.ca/Mountain-Mandalas-Shugendo-Allan-Grapard/dp/1474249000|title=Mountain Mandalas: Shugendo in Kyushu|last=Grapard|first=Allan G.|last2=Rambelli|first2=Fabio|date=2016-02-25|publisher=Bloomsbury Academic|isbn=978-1-4742-4900-3|edition=Illustrated edition|location=London New York (N. Y.)|language=English}}</ref>{{rp|19}}

It was formerly in the countryside in a dense forest of about three hectares and now in the suburbs of the city of {{ill|Fukuoka|af|Fukuoka|an|Fukuoka|ar|فوكوكا|arz|فوكوكا|ast|Fukuoka|az|Fukuoka|azb|فوکوئوکا|ban|Fukuoka|be|Фукуока|bg|Фукуока|bn|ফুকুওকা|br|Fukuoka|bxr|Фукуока|ca|Fukuoka|ce|Фукуока|ceb|Fukuoka Shi|ckb|فوکوئۆکا|cs|Fukuoka|cy|Fukuoka|da|Fukuoka|de|Fukuoka|el|Φουκουόκα|eo|Fukuoka|es|Fukuoka|et|Fukuoka|eu|Fukuoka|fa|فوکوئوکا|fi|Fukuoka|fj|Fukuoka|fo|Fukuoka|fr|Fukuoka|frr|Fukuoka|ga|Fukuoka|gl|Fukuoka|ha|Fukuoka|hak|Fukuoka|he|פוקואוקה|hi|फुकुओका|hr|Fukuoka|hu|Fukuoka|hy|Ֆուկուոկա (քաղաք)|id|Fukuoka|ie|Fukuoka|io|Fukuoka|it|Fukuoka|ja|福岡市|ka|ფუკუოკა|ki|Fukuoka|ko|후쿠오카시|ky|Фукуока|la|Fukuoka|lb|Fukuoka|lt|Fukuoka|lv|Fukuoka|mdf|Фукуока|mg|Fukuoka|mi|Fukuoka|ml|ഫുക്കുഓക്ക|mn|Фүкүока|mr|फुकुओका|ms|Fukuoka|mt|Fukuoka|my|ဖူကူအိုကာမြို့|mzn|فوکوئوکا (شهر)|nl|Fukuoka (stad)|nn|Fukuoka|no|Fukuoka (Fukuoka)|os|Фукуокæ|pl|Fukuoka|pms|Fukuoka|pnb|فکوکا|pnt|Φουκουόκα|ps|فوکویوکا|pt|Fukuoka (cidade)|qu|Fukuoka|ro|Fukuoka|ru|Фукуока|sc|Fukuoka|sco|Fukuoka|sh|Fukuoka|simple|Fukuoka|sk|Fukuoka (Fukuoka)|sq|Fukuoka|sr|Фукуока|su|Fukuoka|sv|Fukuoka|sw|Fukuoka, Fukuoka|szl|Fukuoka|ta|புக்குவோக்கா|tg|Фукуока|th|ฟูกูโอกะ (เมือง)|tl|Fukuoka|tr|Fukuoka|tt|Фукуока|tum|Fukuoka|tw|Fukuoka|udm|Фукуока|uk|Фукуока|ur|فوکوکا|uz|Fukuoka|vep|Fukuok|vi|Fukuoka (thành phố)|vo|Fukuoka|war|Fukuoka|wo|Fukuoka|wuu|福冈市|zh|福岡市|zh_classical|福岡市|zh_min_nan|Hukuoka-chhī|zh_yue|福岡市|qid=Q26600|lt=Fukuoka}} in Japan. There are venerated Emperor {{ill|Emperor Chūai|en|Emperor Chūai|qid=Q179971|lt=Chūai}} and his wife {{ill|Empress Jingū|en|Empress Jingū|qid=Q232803|lt=Jingū}}, whose son {{ill|Emperor Ōjin|en|Emperor Ōjin|qid=Q317997|lt=Ōjin}} is the fifteenth emperor of Japan, as well as the {{ill|Sumiyoshi sanjin}} , sea deities..<ref name="www.ip.kyusan-u.ac.jp" /><ref name="VISIT FUKUOKA -Fukuoka Prefecture Official Travel Guide" /> 

As {{ill|Emperor Chūai|en|Emperor Chūai|qid=Q179971|lt=Emperor Chūai}} found his final resting place here, older texts use the term ''Kashii-{{ill|Miao shrine|en|Miao shrine|qid=Q29043583|lt=byō}}'' ({{Lang|ja|香椎廟}}, " Kashii courtyard ", " Kashii mausoleum ").<ref name="www.ip.kyusan-u.ac.jp">{{Cite web|title=HISTORY|url=http://www.ip.kyusan-u.ac.jp/J/kokubun/kashii/rekishi.html|access-date=2024-03-28|website=www.ip.kyusan-u.ac.jp}}</ref>

Since the {{ill|Nara period|en|Nara period|qid=Q189178|lt=Nara period}}, the shrine has been part of the small group of shrines called ''[[chokusaisha]]'' which on certain specific occasions receive the {{Nihongo|envoys|勅使|Chokushi}} of the ''{{ill|Emperor of Japan|en|Emperor of Japan|qid=Q208233|lt=tennō}}'' . As at the [[Usa Jingū|Usa Hachiman-gū]] shrine (northeast of [[Kyushu|Kyūshū]] ), this happens every ten years in Kashii. The 800m long staircase which leads to the sanctuary is lined with {{ill|Camphor|ar|كافور (مركب كيميائي)|as|কৰ্পূৰ|ast|Alcanfor|azb|کافور|bg|Камфор|bn|কর্পূর|ca|Càmfora|cs|Kafr|da|Kamfer|de|Campher|dv|ކާފޫރު|el|Καμφορά|eo|Kamforo|es|Alcanfor|eu|Kanfor|fa|کافور|fi|Kamferi|fr|Camphre|ga|Camfar|gl|Alcanfor|gu|કપૂર|he|קמפור|hr|Kamfor|hu|Kámfor|hy|Կամֆորա|id|Kapur barus|io|Kamforo|it|Canfora|ja|樟脳|jv|Kapur barus|kcg|A̱bwuncyui|kk|Камфора|kn|ಕರ್ಪೂರ|ko|장뇌|ky|Камфора|la|Camphora|lt|Kamparas|lv|Kampars|mai|कपुर|ml|കർപ്പൂരം (സുഗന്ധദ്രവ്യം)|mr|कापूर|ms|Kapur barus|ne|कपुर|nl|Kamfer|nn|Kamfer|no|Kamfer|pl|Kamfora|pnb|کافور|pt|Cânfora|ro|Camfor|ru|Камфора|sa|कर्पूरम्|sd|ڪافور|sh|Kamfor|simple|Camphor|sk|Gáfor|sl|Kafra|sq|Qafuri|sr|Камфор|su|Kamper|sv|Kamfer|ta|கற்பூரம்|te|కర్పూరం|th|การบูร|tl|Alkampor|tr|Kâfur|ug|كافۇر|uk|Камфора|ur|کافور|uz|Kamfora|vi|Long não|wuu|樟脑|zh|樟腦|zh_yue|樟腦|qid=Q181559|lt=camphor trees}} .

The structure, called {{Nihongo|Kashii style|香椎造|Kashii-zukuri}},<ref>{{Cite web|title=Kashii-zukuri (香椎造)|url=http://www.aisf.or.jp/~jaanus/deta/k/kashiizukuri.htm|access-date=19 novembre 2019|website=www.aisf.or.jp|language=en}}.</ref> of the main building, (the ''[[honden]]'' ) — whose current appearance dates back to the last reconstruction in 1801 — can only be found here. The building is divided into three parts with hinged doors and a roof with many forks ( ''{{ill|Chigi (architecture)|en|Chigi (architecture)|qid=Q262282|lt=chigi}}'' ).<ref name="www.ip.kyusan-u.ac.jp-3">{{Cite web|title=HONDEN|url=http://www.ip.kyusan-u.ac.jp/J/kokubun/kashii/honden.html|access-date=2024-03-28|website=www.ip.kyusan-u.ac.jp}}</ref><ref name="now-2014" /><ref name="VISIT FUKUOKA -Fukuoka Prefecture Official Travel Guide" />

For many generations, the priesthood was reserved for four families who took turns every four years in the exercise of their functions.

Until the middleof the {{ill|20th century|en|20th century|qid=Q6927|lt=20th century}} there were in the vicinity a number of Buddhist temples of the [[Shingon school]] which, as a result of the law of " separation of Shinto and Buddhism » ( ''[[shinbutsu bunri]]'' ,{{Lang|ja|神仏分離}}) of 1868 were destroyed. Today, the only remaining witness to this past where Shintoism and Buddhism were mixed ( ''[[Shinbutsu-shūgō|Shinbutsu shūgō]]'' ,{{Lang|ja|神仏習合|1=Shinbutsu-shūgō}}), is a small temple of the divinity [[Benzaiten]] .

== Historical Background ==
{{ill|Empress Jingū|en|Empress Jingū|qid=Q232803|lt=Empress Jingu}} founded the Kashii gu Shrine around the year 200 AD to honor {{ill|Emperor Chūai|en|Emperor Chūai|qid=Q179971|lt=Emperor Chuai}}, her late husband, who is said to have passed away at this location. The shrine serves as a memorial for not Empress Jingu but their son, Emperor Ojin commemorating three important figures from ancient Japanese tales. While historical records do not definitively confirm their existence the shrine has maintained a connection to Japans lineage.<ref name="now-2014">{{Cite web|last=now|first=fukuoka|date=2014-05-28|title=Kashii-gu: A Shrine with Close Ties to the Imperial Court|url=http://www.fukuoka-now.com/en/kashii-gu-a-shrine-with-close-ties-to-the-imperial-court/|access-date=2024-03-28|website=Fukuoka Now|language=en-US}}</ref><ref name="Let's travel around Japan">{{Cite web|title=Kashiigu shrine (Fukuoka city, Fukuoka Prefecture) - Let's travel around Japan!|url=http://www.travel-around-japan.com/k91-01-07-kashiigu.html|access-date=2024-03-28|website=Let's travel around Japan}}</ref><ref name="VISIT FUKUOKA -Fukuoka Prefecture Official Travel Guide" />

On the site are other small shrines dedicated to the deities {{ill|Inari Ōkami|en|Inari Ōkami|qid=Q719665|lt=Inari}}, Takeuchi Sukune, etc. According to tradition, the legendary Jingū had a Kashii no miya shrine ({{Lang|ja|橿日宮}}) built here in {{ill|200|en|200|qid=Q23813|lt=200}}, when Chūai died in battle against the [[Kumaso]] people. There would have been an ancient sanctuary in the vicinity of this one but there is no historical mention of it before the year {{ill|723|en|723|qid=Q23545|lt=723}} .<ref name="www.ip.kyusan-u.ac.jp" /><ref name="VISIT FUKUOKA -Fukuoka Prefecture Official Travel Guide" />

Records indicate that the shrine was officially established in 724 following an oracle associated with Empress Jingû. Documentation from 728 further confirms the shrines existence during that era emphasizing its importance since its inception. Kashiigu has been acknowledged as a shrine evidenced by visits from imperial messengers every ten years—a tradition upheld throughout centuries.<ref name="Let's travel around Japan" />

A notable tradition that highlights this bond is the visitation by an envoy to Kashii gu Shrine once every ten years. This custom places Kashii gu among a group of 17 shrines across Japan that receive esteemed visits. Over time 138 imperial envoys have visited the shrine. The {{ill|Sandō|en|Sandō}} path leading to the shrine is called "Imperial Envoy Road " and it is lined with 165 camphor trees symbolizing unity among present municipalities, within the prefecture.<ref name="now-2014" /> This is because the shrine is a [[Chokusaisha]].<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ZPUlAQAAIAAJ|title=An Encyclopedia of Shinto: Norman Havens, Nobutaka Inoue. Institute for Japanese Culture and Classics Kokugakuin University, 2006.|accessdate=1 January 2014}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Shinto Jiten (Dictionary of Shinto: 神道事典): Kokugakuin Daigaku Nihon Bunka Kenkyujo (国学院大学日本文化研究所), ed. Tokyo: Kokubundo, 1994.|url=https://www.amazon.com/Shinto-jiten-Japanese-Edition/dp/4335160232|accessdate=1 January 2014}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Jinja jiten (神社辞典)/ Shirai Eiji ; Toki Masanori hen, 1997.|url=http://catalogue.nla.gov.au/Record/70123|accessdate=1 January 2014}}</ref>

== Facilities ==

=== Main hall ===
The main hall of Kashii gu showcases the style known as {{Nihongo|Kashii style|香椎造|Kashii-zukuri}}, a design specific, to this shrine. Constructed in 1801 under the patronage of Nagayori Kuroda, the lord of Chikuzen Province the current structure is believed to be a scaled down version of its form. Despite this the shrine continues to exude a sense of spaciousness and spiritual significance.<ref name="now-2014" /><ref name="VISIT FUKUOKA -Fukuoka Prefecture Official Travel Guide" /><ref name="www.ip.kyusan-u.ac.jp-3" />

There is a sacred [[Shinboku]] tree Ayasugi, a Japanese cedar tree whose seed was buried in the ground by {{ill|Empress Jingū|en|Empress Jingū|qid=Q232803|lt=Empress Jingu}} herself.<ref name="now-2014" /><ref name="Let's travel around Japan" />

The gateway to the area is marked by the Romon gate leading to the core shrine complex. This complex comprises the Honden, Haiden, and Heiden all interconnected and reconstructed in 1801. The architectural style of the shrine, known as "{{Nihongo|Kashii style|香椎造|Kashii-zukuri}}" is distinct and specific to Kashiigu Shrine.<ref name="Let's travel around Japan" /><ref name="VISIT FUKUOKA -Fukuoka Prefecture Official Travel Guide" />

In addition, to its hall, Kashii gu houses many smaller Shrines or Setsumatsusha honoring various deities. Among them is a shrine that worships [[Takenouchi no Sukune]], a figure known for his longevity spanning five imperial reigns. .<ref name="now-2014" /><ref name="www.ip.kyusan-u.ac.jp-2">{{Cite web|title=FUROSUI|url=http://www.ip.kyusan-u.ac.jp/J/kokubun/kashii/furosui.html|access-date=2024-03-28|website=www.ip.kyusan-u.ac.jp}}</ref>

=== Spring of youth ===
The Furôsui Spring (water of youth)<ref name="VISIT FUKUOKA -Fukuoka Prefecture Official Travel Guide" /> lies 500 meters northeast of the shrine within an area. According to legend a [[Takenouchi no Sukune]] who dRank from this spring lived for over three centuries. The water, from this spring is renowned for its purity. Is annually offered to the family during New Years festivities. Visitors can also sample this water at the shrine believed to possess life prolonging qualities.<ref name="Let's travel around Japan" /><ref name="VISIT FUKUOKA -Fukuoka Prefecture Official Travel Guide" /><ref name="now-2014" /><ref name="www.ip.kyusan-u.ac.jp-2" /> Until the [[Meiji Restoration]] there was an annual event of delivering water from it to the {{ill|Emperor of Japan|en|Emperor of Japan|qid=Q208233|lt=Emperor of Japan}} in {{ill|Kyoto|en|Kyoto|qid=Q34600|lt=Kyoto}}.<ref name="www.ip.kyusan-u.ac.jp" /> [[Takenouchi no Sukune]] is said to have lived for centuries from drinking this water<ref name="www.ip.kyusan-u.ac.jp-2" />. The well is recognized as one of Japans 100 springs.<ref name="now-2014" /><ref name="www.ip.kyusan-u.ac.jp-2" /> 

The shrines grounds cover an area 400x200 meters with the former being the [[:en:X axis|X axis]] or west to east, and the latter or 200 meters being the [[:en:Y axis|Y axis]] of north to south. The western part of the precinct includes an approach spanning 120 meters. Moreover there is a pathway stretching one kilometer on the west side of the JR railway station lined with camphor trees leading to the shrines entrance.<ref name="Let's travel around Japan" />

There is a garden nearby full of Iris flowers.<ref name="Let's travel around Japan" />
